critic.argument: This claim is a textbook case of a single-source, low-engagement artifact being over-interpreted as a finding. The entire 'cluster' is one RSS item whose only substantive content is a throwaway line: 'aria-describedby isn't always enough.' That sentence is generic, widely known in web accessibility circles, and would be repeated almost verbatim in any introductory talk on ARIA. The document supplies no failure mode, no code, no correction, no context about the tooltip, the user, the assistive technology, or the observed defect. As a result, the claim that the author 'shipped a tooltip implementation relying on aria-describedby and later concluded that this attribute alone does not produce an accessible tooltip' is not an observation from the text but a narrative reconstruction imposed on it. The framing line does not even assert that the author made a mistake; it could just as easily be a general caution, a quote from someone else, or a note to self. Circularity enters when the text is read through the claim's own expectation of a personal lesson. Thinness is fatal: n=1, low engagement, no corroborating or contradicting sources, and no testable specifics. The move to call it a 'small artifact of hands-on software craftsmanship' then to declare it 'too thin to inform the brief's leadership, estimation, AI-agent, or teaching themes' admits the evidence cannot bear the weight of any substantive inference. What remains is a lexical coincidence: the words 'tooltip' and 'accessibility' appear together in a title, and the phrase 'aria-describedby isn't always enough' is a recognizable accessibility aphorism. That is not a finding; it is a triviality dressed as a finding. The claim does not survive scrutiny.
